Quick numbers and assumptions (draft — will refine once replay lands):

Assumptions: 1M generated tokens; model footprint similar to Llama-2-70B family; batching configured to 32-token windows average, and 45% cache hit for prefix reuse. Networking + infra overhead ~8% of compute cost.

Preliminary per-1M token effective cost (USD)
- Redwood Hosted (default quant/throughput): $20 per 1M tokens
- Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity, amortized infra): $11 per 1M tokens*
- HyperscaleX (public pricing, fp16): ~$27 per 1M tokens
- CloudTensor (vendor quote, quantized): ~$16 per 1M tokens

*Dedicated assumes 3-month commit and 70% utilization in the POC window. If utilization drops to 40% the effective cost moves toward $16/1M.

Key tradeoffs and notes
- Caching reduces effective billed tokens by direct hit rate; at 45% hit we see ~36% reduction in billed tokens after accounting for cache fill traffic. That drives Hosted cost down proportionally for repeat-heavy workloads.
- Batching improves throughput but increases tail latency; we tune batching windows to meet p99 SLO. For this workload, tuned batching reduces compute cost ~20–30% vs naive single-request runs while keeping p99 within 300ms.
- Quantization: CloudTensor quoted smaller units via aggressive int8 which reduces cost but can increase generation latency and slightly degrade some instruction-following outputs. HyperscaleX fp16 maintains quality but higher cost. Redwood supports quantized variants and can recommend per-prompt profiles.

Attachments: rdw-1m-token-snapshot.csv (detailed calc), short-econ-notes.pdf (one-pager).

Next step (for Sasha): we’ll run the baseline 1M tokens and the cached scenario; after the two runs I’ll produce a side-by-side table with actual measured token counts, GPU hours, and effective per-1M cost.
